questions.q: A team needs to run T-SQL queries directly against structured tables with strong schema enforcement, and doesn't need Spark. Which Fabric item is the better fit?
options: A Warehouse
A Lakehouse
An Eventhouse
A Dataflow Gen2
questions.explain: A Warehouse is SQL-first with strong schema enforcement; a Lakehouse is the Spark/file-first option — swapping the two is the classic lookalike-item-type trap.

questions.q: A team wants to query data that lives in another team's lakehouse without copying it into their own workspace. What Fabric feature enables this?
options: A OneLake shortcut
A deployment pipeline
A sensitivity label
A workspace role change
questions.explain: Shortcuts reference data in place across OneLake without duplicating it — a deployment pipeline and sensitivity labels solve entirely different problems.

questions.q: A semantic model in Direct Lake Mode is showing slower-than-expected query performance after a large number of small file writes to the underlying Delta table. What's the most likely cause?
options: File fragmentation from many small writes, which Direct Lake Mode is sensitive to until the files are optimized/compacted
Direct Lake Mode is incompatible with Delta tables entirely
The semantic model needs a sensitivity label applied
The workspace role is set too narrowly
questions.explain: Direct Lake Mode reads Delta Parquet files directly, so file fragmentation from frequent small writes directly affects its query performance — this is a Domain 1 performance-characteristics question, not a security one.

questions.q: An Eventstream needs to ingest data from an external IoT source and land it in a KQL database for near-real-time querying. What's the correct pairing?
options: Eventstream as the ingestion path, an Eventhouse/KQL database as the destination
A Dataflow Gen2 as the ingestion path, a Warehouse as the destination
A Data pipeline as the only component needed, with no database
A Lakehouse Files folder as the destination, bypassing any database
questions.explain: Eventstreams are built for streaming ingestion, and an Eventhouse/KQL database is the destination built for near-real-time querying — matching the right tool to each half of the scenario.

questions.q: A dimension table needs to track history when a customer's address changes, implemented as a targeted update rather than a full table rewrite. Which pattern does this describe?
options: An SCD Type 2 update implemented as a MERGE INTO a Delta table
A OneLake data access role
A deployment pipeline stage gate
A KQL summarize query
questions.explain: This is the SCD Type 2-as-merge pattern from this course's Chapter 1 (Lesson 8) and the Databricks & Delta Lake course's MERGE INTO lesson — a Domain 2 data-transformation concept, not a security or deployment one.

questions.q: A solution must stay within a single Fabric capacity for cost reasons, and a scenario asks which SKU consideration matters most. What's the relevant concern?
options: Whether the capacity's compute (CU) limits can handle the combined workload of every item assigned to it
Whether the capacity has a sensitivity label applied
Whether the capacity supports Git integration at all
Whether the capacity has row-level security enabled
questions.explain: Capacity/SKU sizing is about compute unit limits across everything assigned to that capacity — a Domain 1/3 overlap concern, distinct from security or Git features.

questions.q: An analyst needs read access to one table in a shared lakehouse, and nothing else in the workspace. Which control is correctly scoped?
options: A OneLake data access role on that table's folder
A workspace Contributor role
Sharing the entire lakehouse item
A deployment pipeline promotion
questions.explain: This repeats Lesson 35's narrowest-control pattern: a OneLake data access role scopes access to exactly the needed data, unlike the broader options.

questions.q: A team wants a paper trail of who approved a notebook change before it reaches Production, plus the ability to test it in a Test workspace first. What combination answers this?
options: Git integration plus a deployment pipeline
The Monitoring Hub alone
A sensitivity label on the notebook
Row-level security on the notebook's output table
questions.explain: This repeats Lesson 36's pattern: Git integration provides the trail, deployment pipelines provide the Dev/Test/Prod gate — the Monitoring Hub answers a different kind of question entirely.

questions.q: A question states a workload 'must always use the cheapest possible SKU regardless of workload size,' and asks whether this is a valid Fabric capacity planning principle. What's the correct read?
options: No — this is absolute wording bait; the right SKU depends on the actual workload's compute needs, not a blanket 'always cheapest' rule
Yes — Fabric always recommends the cheapest SKU in every case
Yes, because sensitivity labels determine SKU cost
No — because Fabric has no concept of SKUs at all
questions.explain: This combines Lesson 37's absolute-wording trap with real capacity-planning content: the correct SKU is workload-dependent, not a blanket rule — recognizing the trap pattern is the actual test here.
